In chest trauma, rib fractures are sought with the bone window, following each rib from the posterior articulation to the cartilage: non-displaced fractures are easy to miss (here the lowest one). Count the ribs starting from the first (the one reaching the manubrium below the clavicle), from the rib heads or in a 3D reconstruction: in fields of view that start at the apex it is easy to skip the 1st rib and be off by one. Three or more contiguous ribs fractured in two or more places make a flail chest; fractures of the low left ribs prompt a search for splenic injury, those of the first ribs for injuries of the great vessels.
Pneumothorax in the supine patient collects anteriorly and along the border of the heart and diaphragm (deep sulcus): on radiography it is often occult, on CT it appears as air without lung markings beyond the visceral pleural line. Even if small it must be communicated immediately: it can grow, especially with positive-pressure ventilation or air transport.
Extrapleural hematoma forms a lens with obtuse angles between the displaced rib and the lung and does not shift with position, unlike effusion. Pulmonary contusion appears within a few hours as ground glass or non-segmental consolidation below the area of impact and improves in a few days; if it worsens or becomes cavitated, think of laceration or pneumonia.
